title: Cervus Silviae. Prima caedes
titleEn: Silvia's Stag and the First Bloodshed — Aeneid VII.475–600
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: While Turnus rouses the Rutulians, Allecto turns to the Trojans with a new trick. Ascanius is out hunting along the shore, and she maddens his hounds and sets them on the scent of a stag. This is no ordinary animal: a tame stag of great beauty, taken from its mother as a fawn and raised by the sons of Tyrrhus, the king's chief herdsman, and petted by their sister Silvia, who garlands its antlers, combs it and washes it in the spring; it roams the woods by day and comes home of its own accord at night. The hounds start it as it cools itself by the river, and Ascanius, eager for glory, shoots, and a god guides the arrow through its flanks. The wounded creature staggers home to its stall, bleeding and moaning like a person begging for help. Silvia calls out the country people, who come running with whatever they can find, firebrands and knotted clubs, and Tyrrhus leaves his wood-splitting with his axe in his hand. Then Allecto climbs to the roof of the farmstead and blows the herdsmen's call on a horn with a voice from hell, heard as far away as Diana's lake and the river Nar, so that mothers clutch their babies. The farmers gather; the Trojans pour out of their camp to help Ascanius; and the brawl becomes a battle, with drawn swords in place of stakes, rising like a sea that swells under the first wind. The first to fall are Almo, Tyrrhus's eldest son, shot through the throat, and old Galaesus, the most just man in Italy and once the richest, killed as he stepped between the lines to make peace. Allecto reports her success to Juno and offers to draw the neighbouring cities into the war, but Juno has had enough of her and sends her back below; she sinks into the earth at Amsanctus, a reeking valley in the middle of Italy where the underworld breathes out. Juno puts the finishing touch to the war herself. The herdsmen carry their dead into the city; Turnus stokes their fears; the families of the women Amata led into the woods join them; and they all, against every omen, besiege Latinus's palace demanding war. The old king stands like a rock in the sea, until he sees that Juno's will is going to prevail. Then he calls the gods to witness, foretells that the people and Turnus will pay for this sacrilege, and, saying that all he loses is a peaceful death, shuts himself in his palace and lets go the reins of government.
part: Silvia's Stag and the First Bloodshed (VII.475–600)

sentences.t:
Dum Turnus Rutulos animis audacibus implet,
Allecto in Teucros Stygiis se concitat alis,
arte nova speculata locum, quo litore pulcher
insidiis cursuque feras agitabat Iulus.
sentences.l:
While Turnus the Rutulians with spirits bold fills,
Allecto against the Teucrians on Stygian wings speeds herself,
with new craft having spied out the place, on what shore the handsome
with snares and running the wild beasts was hunting, Iulus.
sentences.i: While Turnus fills the Rutulians with bold spirit, Allecto speeds on her Stygian wings against the Teucrians, with a fresh trick in mind, having marked out the stretch of shore where handsome Iulus was hunting wild beasts with snares and with the chase.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Dum… implet', 'while he fills', 'dum' with the present indicative, as usual for 'while'. 'Animis audacibus', ablative of means, 'with bold spirit'. 'Se concitat', 'rouses herself', 'speeds'. 'Stygiis… alis', 'on Stygian wings', from the underworld river, her home. 'Arte nova', 'by a new device': her third stroke, after Amata and Turnus. 'Speculata', perfect participle of the deponent 'speculor', 'having spied out', with 'locum' as its object. 'Quo litore', 'on which shore': the relative has drawn the noun into its own clause, so 'locum, quo litore' means 'the place, the shore on which'. 'Insidiis cursuque', ablatives of means: traps or ambush, and running the game down. 'Agitabat', imperfect, 'was hunting'. 'Iulus' is Ascanius, Aeneas's son; the name ties him to the Julian house. In the verse 'Teucros' has two syllables and 'Iulus' three, Ĭ-ū-lus.

sentences.i: Here the maiden of Cocytus casts a sudden frenzy on his hounds and touches their nostrils with a scent they knew, so that they would give hot chase to the stag;
sentences.n: 'Hic', 'here', 'at this point'. 'Subitam… rabiem', 'a sudden madness', the adjective held apart from its noun by 'canibus'. 'Canibus', dative with 'obicit', 'throws in the way of', 'casts upon'. 'Cocytia virgo', 'the Cocytian maiden', Allecto, named from Cocytus, the underworld river of wailing; 'virgo' because the Furies are the unwedded daughters of Night. 'Naris' is accusative plural of 'naris', 'nostril', with Greenough's '-is' for '-es' (you'll see this constantly). 'Noto… odore', ablative of means, 'with a familiar scent', the scent of deer that hounds know. 'Ut… agerent', a purpose clause; the imperfect subjunctive follows the historic presents 'obicit' and 'contingit', which may take secondary sequence, as here. 'Ardentes', 'burning', 'eager', agrees with the hounds, the understood subject.

sentences.t:
quae prima laborum
causa fuit belloque animos accendit agrestis.
sentences.l:
and this the first of the toils
cause was, and for war kindled the rustic spirits.
sentences.i: and this was the first cause of all the hardships to come, and it set the country people's hearts ablaze for war.
sentences.n: 'Quae', a connecting relative, 'and this', agreeing with 'causa' rather than with the whole act it points back to (the pattern seen often since the pilot). 'Prima laborum causa', 'the first cause of the toils', the sufferings of the coming war. Virgil marks beginnings this way: compare 4.169–170, of the day in the cave, 'ille dies primus leti primusque malorum causa fuit'. 'Bello', dative of purpose, 'for war'. 'Accendit' is perfect here, beside 'fuit'. 'Animos… agrestis', 'the rustic spirits', with 'agrestis' accusative plural (= 'agrestes') agreeing with 'animos'.

sentences.t:
Cervus erat forma praestanti et cornibus ingens,
Tyrrhidae pueri quem matris ab ubere raptum
nutribant Tyrrhusque pater, cui regia parent
armenta et late custodia credita campi.
sentences.l:
A stag there was, of form outstanding and in its horns huge,
which the Tyrrhid boys, from its mother's udder snatched,
were rearing, and Tyrrhus their father, whom the royal obey
herds, and to whom far and wide the keeping was entrusted of the plain.
sentences.i: There was a stag of rare beauty, with a great spread of antlers, which the sons of Tyrrhus had taken from its mother's udder and were rearing, they and their father Tyrrhus, whom the king's herds obey and to whom the charge of the broad lands had been given.
sentences.n: 'Forma praestanti', ablative of quality, 'of outstanding form'; 'cornibus ingens', ablative of respect, 'huge in its horns'. 'Tyrrhidae', 'sons of Tyrrhus', a Greek patronymic in '-ides' (nominative plural), used with 'pueri' as an adjective. 'Quem… raptum', 'which, snatched…', the participle agreeing with the relative. 'Nutribant' is the old imperfect in '-ibam' for '-iebam' (= 'nutriebant'), an archaism Virgil allows himself (compare 'lenibat', 6.468). 'Cui… parent', 'whom… obey': 'pareo' takes the dative. The same 'cui' serves 'credita (est)', 'to whom was entrusted'. 'Custodia… campi', 'the guarding of the plain', with 'late', 'far and wide': Tyrrhus is the king's chief herdsman.

sentences.t:
Adsuetum imperiis soror omni Silvia cura
mollibus intexens ornabat cornua sertis
pectebatque ferum puroque in fonte lavabat.
sentences.l:
It, used to commands, their sister, with every care, Silvia,
twining it with soft garlands, was decking its horns,
and was combing the wild creature, and in a pure spring was washing it.
sentences.i: Their sister Silvia tended it with every care, now that it had learned to obey, twining soft garlands to deck its antlers, combing the wild creature and washing it in a clear spring.
sentences.n: 'Adsuetum imperiis', 'used to commands', agreeing with the stag, understood as the object of the verbs; 'imperiis' is dative with 'adsuetus'. Greenough leaves 'ad-' unassimilated (familiar 'assuetum'), as again at 490; the word has three syllables, ad-suē-tum, the u of 'sue-' being a consonant. 'Soror', the boys' sister. 'Silvia', 'girl of the woods', a speaking name, and the name too of Rhea Silvia, mother of Romulus. 'Omni… cura', ablative of manner. 'Mollibus… sertis' framing the line, ablative of means with 'intexens', 'weaving (them) about with soft garlands'. 'Ferum', 'the wild thing', the adjective 'ferus' used as a noun: the creature is wild by nature and tame by her care. The imperfects describe what she used to do.

sentences.t:
Ille, manum patiens mensaeque adsuetus erili,
errabat silvis rursusque ad limina nota
ipse domum sera quamvis se nocte ferebat.
sentences.l:
It, the hand enduring and used to the table of its master,
would wander in the woods, and back to the threshold it knew,
of itself, home, late though at night, it would carry itself.
sentences.i: Tame to the hand and used to its master's table, it would roam the woods, and then of its own accord, however late at night, would make its way home again to the door it knew.
sentences.n: 'Ille', 'it', the stag. 'Manum patiens', 'enduring the hand': 'patiens' as a participle takes an accusative object (as an adjective it would take a genitive). 'Mensae… erili', dative with 'adsuetus', 'its master's table'; 'erilis' is from 'erus', 'master' (familiar 'herilis'). 'Silvis', ablative of place. 'Ipse', 'of itself', unbidden. 'Ad limina nota' and 'domum' (accusative of place to which, without a preposition, as usual with 'domus') both name the goal. 'Sera quamvis… nocte', 'though late at night', with 'quamvis' postponed. 'Se… ferebat', 'betook itself'. The imperfects are of habit.

sentences.t:
Hunc procul errantem rabidae venantis Iuli
commovere canes, fluvio cum forte secundo
deflueret ripaque aestus viridante levaret.
sentences.l:
It, far off wandering, the maddened of the hunting Iulus
started, hounds, when by chance down the favouring river
it was floating, and on the bank the heat, the green, was easing.
sentences.i: As it wandered far from home, the maddened hounds of Iulus, out hunting, started it, just when it chanced to be drifting downstream with the current and easing the heat on the green bank.
sentences.n: 'Hunc', the stag, object of 'commovere'. 'Rabidae… canes' framing the clause, the hounds Allecto has maddened. 'Venantis Iuli', 'of Iulus hunting', genitive of the present participle of the deponent 'venor'. 'Commovere' = 'commoverunt' ('-ere' for '-erunt', which you'll see constantly), 'started', roused from cover, the hunter's word. 'Cum… deflueret… levaret', 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive, describing the circumstances. 'Fluvio… secundo', 'on the following river', downstream, with the current. 'Ripa… viridante', 'on the green bank', ablative of place ('rīpā', long-long). 'Iuli' has three syllables, Ĭ-ū-lī. 'Aestus', accusative plural, 'the heats'. 'Errantem' (493) picks up 'errabat' (491): the stag's harmless wandering is what exposes it.

sentences.t:
Ipse etiam, eximiae laudis succensus amore,
Ascanius curvo direxit spicula cornu;
sentences.l:
Himself too, with love of outstanding praise fired,
Ascanius from his curved bow aimed shafts;
sentences.i: Ascanius himself, fired by a longing for rare glory, aimed his arrows from his curving bow;
sentences.n: 'Ipse etiam', 'he himself too', the boy as well as his hounds. 'Eximiae laudis… amore', 'with love of outstanding praise', an objective genitive. 'Succensus', 'kindled', perfect participle of 'succendo'. 'Curvo… cornu', 'from the curved horn': bows were made of horn, so the material names the thing (metonymy). 'Spicula', 'shafts', 'darts', the plural for the arrow he shoots. 'Direxit', 'aimed'; the Latin Library's 'derexit' is only a spelling.

sentences.t:
nec dextrae erranti deus afuit, actaque multo
perque uterum sonitu perque ilia venit harundo.
sentences.l:
nor from his right hand, unsure, was a god absent, and driven with much
both through the belly, noise, and through the flanks came the reed.
sentences.i: nor did a god fail his uncertain hand, and the arrow went whirring loudly through the belly and through the flanks.
sentences.n: 'Nec… deus afuit', litotes: 'nor was a god absent', that is, a god was there to guide the shot; 'dextrae erranti', dative with 'afuit'. 'Erranti', 'straying', 'unsure': the hand that might have missed meets the stag that 'wandered' ('errabat', 'errantem'). Virgil does not name the god; the reader knows who is at work. 'Acta… harundo', 'the driven reed', the arrow, whose shaft is a reed. 'Multo… sonitu', ablative of manner, 'with much noise'. 'Perque… perque', 'both through… and through', the double '-que' flagged in the pilot. 'Uterum', 'belly'; 'ilia', 'flanks', 'groin'. Ancient readers knew another deer whose killing cost dear: the stag of Artemis that Agamemnon shot, for which the goddess held the Greek fleet at Aulis.

sentences.t:
Saucius at quadrupes nota intra tecta refugit
successitque gemens stabulis questuque cruentus
atque imploranti similis tectum omne replebat.
sentences.l:
But wounded, the four-footed one within its known roof fled back,
and came, groaning, up to its stalls, and with lament, bloodied,
and like one imploring, the whole house it was filling.
sentences.i: But the wounded creature fled back to the house it knew and came moaning to its stall, and, bleeding and like someone begging for help, filled the whole house with its cries.
sentences.n: 'At', 'but', is postponed to second place. 'Quadrupes', 'the four-footed one', the beast (the Latin Library's 'quadripes' is a spelling). 'Nota intra tecta', the preposition set between adjective and noun. 'Successit… stabulis', 'came up to the stalls', dative with a compound verb. 'Questu', ablative of means with 'replebat', 'with its lament'. 'Cruentus', 'bloodied'. 'Imploranti similis', 'like one imploring', the dative with 'similis': the beast almost speaks. The tense moves from the perfects to the imperfect 'replebat': the crying goes on.

sentences.t:
Silvia prima soror, palmis percussa lacertos,
auxilium vocat et duros conclamat agrestis.
sentences.l:
Silvia first, the sister, with her palms struck on her arms,
for help calls and with a shout rouses the hardy country folk.
sentences.i: Silvia, their sister, is the first: beating her arms with her palms, she calls for help and shouts to rouse the hardy country folk.
sentences.n: 'Prima', 'first' to see and cry out. 'Palmis percussa lacertos', 'struck as to her arms with her palms': a passive participle with an accusative of the part affected, the Greek 'middle' use that you'll meet often. Beating the arms or breast is a gesture of grief. 'Auxilium vocat', 'calls for help'. 'Conclamat', 'calls together with a shout'. 'Agrestis' = 'agrestes', accusative plural, here a noun, 'the country folk'; 'duros', 'hardy'.

sentences.t:
Olli, pestis enim tacitis latet aspera silvis,
inprovisi adsunt, hic torre armatus obusto,
stipitis hic gravidi nodis:
sentences.l:
They (for the plague in the silent lurks, fierce, woods)
unlooked-for are there, this one with a brand armed, burnt at the tip,
this one with a heavy stake's knots:
sentences.i: They are there before anyone could expect them (for the cruel pest lurks in the silent woods), one armed with a fire-hardened brand, another with a heavy knotted club:
sentences.n: 'Olli', the old form of 'illi', 'they', a word with an Ennian ring. 'Pestis… aspera', 'the cruel plague', Allecto, hiding in the woods and driving them on; the parenthesis explains why they come so fast. 'Tacitis… silvis', ablative of place. 'Inprovisi', 'unforeseen', 'before they are looked for', with Greenough's 'in-' left unassimilated (familiar 'improvisi'). 'Hic… hic', 'this one… that one'. 'Torre… obusto', 'with a brand burnt at the end', a stake hardened in the fire. 'Stipitis… gravidi nodis', 'with the knots of a heavy stake', a knotted cudgel: 'nodis' is the ablative of means, 'stipitis' depends on it.

sentences.t:
quod cuique repertum
rimanti, telum ira facit.
sentences.l:
what to each was found
as he searched, a weapon anger makes.
sentences.i: whatever each man found as he rummaged about, his anger turned into a weapon.
sentences.n: 'Quod cuique repertum (est) rimanti', 'what was found by each as he searched': 'cuique' is a dative of the agent with the perfect participle (poetic), and 'rimanti' agrees with it. The relative clause comes first and its antecedent is left out: '(that thing) anger makes a weapon'. 'Telum' is the predicate. Compare 1.150, 'furor arma ministrat', 'fury supplies the weapons': the same thought.

sentences.t:
Vocat agmina Tyrrhus,
quadrifidam quercum cuneis ut forte coactis
scindebat, rapta spirans immane securi.
sentences.l:
Calls up the bands Tyrrhus,
a four-cleft oak with wedges, as it chanced, driven in,
he was splitting, his axe snatched up, breathing savagely.
sentences.i: Tyrrhus calls out the bands, snatching up his axe and panting fiercely, just as he happened to be splitting an oak into four with wedges hammered in.
sentences.n: 'Vocat agmina', 'calls out the companies', musters his men. 'Ut forte… scindebat', 'as by chance he was splitting', 'ut' with the indicative meaning 'as', 'just as'. 'Quadrifidam', 'four-cleft', proleptic: split into four by the action of the verb. 'Cuneis… coactis', ablative of means, 'with wedges driven in'. 'Rapta… securi', ablative absolute, 'his axe snatched up'; 'securi' is the ablative of the i-stem 'securis'. 'Spirans immane', 'breathing monstrously', the neuter adjective used as an adverb (an internal accusative), a Greek-style idiom you will meet again.

sentences.t:
At saeva e speculis tempus dea nacta nocendi
ardua tecta petit stabuli et de culmine summo
pastorale canit signum cornuque recurvo
Tartaream intendit vocem, qua protinus omne
contremuit nemus et silvae insonuere profundae;
sentences.l:
But the savage, from her lookouts the time, goddess, having found for harming,
the high roof seeks of the steading, and from the topmost ridge
the herdsmen's sounds signal, and on the horn curved back
a Tartarean strains voice, at which at once all
shuddered the grove, and the woods resounded, deep;
sentences.i: But the cruel goddess, seeing from her lookout that the moment for harm had come, makes for the high roof of the farmstead and from its topmost ridge sounds the herdsmen's call, straining a voice of Tartarus through the curling horn, at which every grove shuddered at once and the deep forests rang;
sentences.n: 'Saeva… dea', Allecto, the adjective set well apart from its noun. 'E speculis', 'from her watch-places', her vantage points. 'Tempus… nacta nocendi', 'having found the time for doing harm': 'nacta' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'nanciscor', 'nocendi' the genitive of the gerund. 'Stabuli', the herdsmen's steading. 'Pastorale… signum', the shepherds' call to arms, the country alarm. 'Canit', 'sounds', used of instruments. 'Cornu… recurvo', ablative, 'on the back-curved horn', a cow-horn bugle. 'Tartaream… vocem', 'a voice of Tartarus', the deepest hell. 'Intendit', 'stretches', 'strains'. 'Qua', 'at which', the sound. 'Contremuit… insonuere', perfects of the instant effect ('insonuere' = 'insonuerunt'). The Homeric model is Strife, sent by Zeus to stand on a ship and raise a great shrill cry that puts war into the Greeks' hearts (Iliad 11.3–14).

sentences.t:
audiit et Triviae longe lacus, audiit amnis
sulfurea Nar albus aqua fontesque Velini,
et trepidae matres pressere ad pectora natos.
sentences.l:
heard it too Trivia's, far off, lake, heard it the river,
with sulphurous water white, Nar, and the springs of Velinus,
and anxious mothers pressed to their breasts their children.
sentences.i: Far away, Trivia's lake heard it; the Nar heard it, a river white with sulphurous water, and the springs of Velinus; and frightened mothers clutched their children to their breasts.
sentences.n: 'Audiit… audiit', anaphora: the sound spreading across Italy. 'Triviae… lacus', 'the lake of Trivia', Diana as goddess of the crossroads; it is the lake below her grove at Aricia (Lake Nemi), in the Alban hills. 'Amnis… Nar', 'the river Nar', the noun and its name in apposition. 'Sulfurea… albus aqua', 'white with sulphurous water', ablative of cause; the Nar runs pale with sulphur on its way to the Tiber. 'Fontes Velini', 'the springs of Velinus', the lake in Sabine country whose waters feed the Nar. Both lie far inland: hyperbole, the horn of hell heard through half of Italy. 'Pressere' = 'presserunt'. The frightened mothers are said to come from Apollonius's Argonautica (Book 4), where the hiss of the dragon that guards the fleece wakes mothers, who clutch their infants.

sentences.t:
Tum vero ad vocem celeres, qua bucina signum
dira dedit, raptis concurrunt undique telis
indomiti agricolae; nec non et Troïa pubes
Ascanio auxilium castris effundit apertis.
sentences.l:
Then indeed toward the sound, swift, where the horn its signal,
dread, gave, weapons snatched up, run together from all sides
the untamed farmers; and no less the Trojan youth
to Ascanius help pours out, the camp thrown open.
sentences.i: Then indeed the wild farmers come running from every side, snatching up their weapons, toward the sound where the dread horn had given its signal; and the young men of Troy as well throw open their camp and pour out to help Ascanius.
sentences.n: 'Ad vocem… qua', 'toward the sound… where'; 'qua' is the adverb 'where', 'by which way'. 'Bucina', a curved horn or trumpet. 'Celeres', 'swift', an adjective where English would use an adverb. 'Raptis… telis', ablative absolute. 'Indomiti', 'untamed', unbroken men. 'Nec non et', 'and also', a double negative making a positive, a favourite turn of Virgil's. 'Troïa' is the adjective 'Trojan', three syllables, as Greenough's diaeresis shows. 'Pubes', collective, 'the young men'. 'Ascanio', dative of advantage. 'Auxilium… effundit', 'pours out help', the youth pouring itself out as aid. 'Castris… apertis', ablative absolute, 'the camp thrown open'.

sentences.t: Direxere acies.
sentences.l: They drew up the lines.
sentences.i: They formed their battle lines.
sentences.n: 'Direxere' = 'direxerunt' (the '-ere' perfect again), 'set straight', 'drew up'; the Latin Library's 'derexere' is a spelling. 'Acies', the battle lines. Two words, and the brawl becomes a war.

sentences.t:
Non iam certamine agresti,
stipitibus duris agitur sudibusve praeustis,
sed ferro ancipiti decernunt atraque late
horrescit strictis seges ensibus aeraque fulgent
sole lacessita et lucem sub nubila iactant:
sentences.l:
No longer in a rustic contest,
with hard stakes is it waged or poles hardened in the fire,
but with two-edged steel they decide it, and dark far and wide
bristles, with drawn, the crop, swords, and the bronze gleams,
by the sun provoked, and its light up under the clouds throws:
sentences.i: It is no longer a country brawl, fought with hard cudgels and fire-hardened poles; now they settle it with two-edged steel, far and wide the drawn swords bristle like a dark field of grain, and the bronze flashes as the sun strikes it and flings its light up to the clouds:
sentences.n: 'Agitur', impersonal passive, 'it is carried on', 'the fight is fought'. 'Sudibus… praeustis', 'with stakes burnt at the tip' (compare 'torre obusto', 506), 'praeustis' scanned prae-us-tis, with 'prae' shortened before the vowel; '-ve', 'or'. 'Ferro ancipiti', 'with two-headed steel', blades with two edges. 'Decernunt', 'they decide (the issue)'. 'Atra… seges', 'a dark crop', of swords: the field of blades 'bristles' ('horrescit') like standing grain. Homer's battle 'bristled with long spears' (Iliad 13.339). 'Aera', 'the bronzes', armour and weapons, neuter plural of 'aes', subject of 'fulgent' and 'iactant'. 'Lacessita', 'provoked', struck by the sun. 'Sub nubila', 'up toward the clouds'; 'sub' with the accusative of motion. The gleam of bronze reaching heaven is Homeric too (Iliad 2.455–458).

sentences.t:
fluctus uti primo coepit cum albescere vento,
paulatim sese tollit mare et altius undas
erigit, inde imo consurgit ad aethera fundo.
sentences.l:
as, when a wave at the first wind begins to whiten,
little by little the sea lifts itself, and higher its waves
raises, then from its lowest depth surges up to the sky.
sentences.i: just as, when a wave begins to whiten at the first breath of wind, the sea little by little heaves itself up and lifts its waves higher, and then rises from its deepest bed to the sky.
sentences.n: A simile of growth, matching the war's: brawl, then battle. 'Uti… cum', 'as when'; 'uti' is an old form of 'ut'. 'Fluctus' is nominative, subject of 'coepit'. 'Sese' is long-long, 'mare' short-short. 'Primo… vento', 'at the first wind'. 'Albescere', an inceptive in '-sco', 'to grow white'. 'Imo… fundo', ablative of separation, 'from the lowest bottom'. 'Aethera', Greek accusative singular of 'aether', 'the upper sky'. The model is Homer's swell at Iliad 4.422–428, wave on wave rising at sea and then breaking on the shore, as the Greek ranks move into battle.

sentences.i: Here, in front of the foremost rank, a young man is laid low by a whistling arrow: Almo, who had been the eldest of the sons of Tyrrhus;
sentences.n: 'Primam ante aciem', the preposition between adjective and noun. 'Stridente sagitta', ablative of means, 'by a hissing arrow'. 'Natorum… maximus', 'the greatest of the sons', that is, the eldest ('maximus natu'); the genitive is partitive. 'Fuerat', pluperfect, 'had been': by the time the clause is finished, he is no more. Almo bears the name of a small river just south of Rome. 'Sternitur', historic present, 'is laid low'. The archer is not named.

sentences.t:
haesit enim sub gutture volnus et udae
vocis iter tenuemque inclusit sanguine vitam.
sentences.l:
for stuck under the throat the wound, and of the moist
voice the path and his thin life it shut in with blood.
sentences.i: for the wound lodged under his throat and choked with blood the passage of his liquid voice and his slender life.
sentences.n: 'Haesit… volnus', 'the wound stuck', the wound standing for the arrow that made it; 'volnus' is Greenough's old spelling of 'vulnus'. 'Udae vocis iter', 'the path of the moist voice', the windpipe. 'Tenuem… vitam', 'thin life', the breath, life as air. 'Inclusit… sanguine', 'shut in with blood', the one verb governing both 'iter' and 'vitam'.

sentences.t:
Corpora multa virum circa seniorque Galaesus,
dum paci medium se offert, iustissimus unus
qui fuit Ausoniisque olim ditissimus arvis:
sentences.l:
Bodies many of men around, and the elder Galaesus,
while for peace in the middle he offers himself, most just the one
who was, and in Ausonian once the richest fields:
sentences.i: Around him lie many bodies of men, and old Galaesus, struck down as he put himself between the sides to plead for peace, who was the one most just of men and once the wealthiest in the fields of Ausonia:
sentences.n: The verb is left out, to be taken from 'sternitur' (533): '(are laid low)'. 'Virum', the old genitive plural ('virorum'), the pattern flagged in the pilot. 'Circa', adverb, 'around'. 'Senior', 'elderly', a comparative with the sense of the positive. 'Dum… se offert', 'dum' with the present, 'while he offers himself'. 'Paci', dative of purpose, 'for peace'. 'Medium', 'in the middle', between the two sides. 'Iustissimus unus qui fuit', 'who was the one most just', 'unus' strengthening the superlative; Virgil used the same words of Rhipeus at the fall of Troy, 2.426–427, 'iustissimus unus qui fuit in Teucris'. 'Ausoniis… arvis', 'in the Ausonian fields', ablative of place; Ausonia is Italy.

sentences.t:
quinque greges illi balantum, quina redibant
armenta, et terram centum vertebat aratris.
sentences.l:
five flocks to him of bleaters, five returned
herds, and the earth with a hundred he turned ploughs.
sentences.i: five flocks of bleating sheep were his, five herds of cattle came home to him, and he turned the soil with a hundred ploughs.
sentences.n: 'Illi', dative of possession, 'to him (there were)': the flocks were his. 'Balantum', 'of the bleaters', sheep, the genitive plural of the present participle used as a noun, in the poetic form '-um' for '-ium'. 'Quina', a distributive, 'five apiece', used by the poets simply for 'five' to vary 'quinque'. 'Redibant', 'came back', from pasture in the evening. 'Vertebat', 'he turned' the soil, ploughed it. The imperfects describe the life that has just ended; the wealth sharpens the loss.

sentences.t:
Atque ea per campos aequo dum Marte geruntur,
promissi dea facta potens, ubi sanguine bellum
imbuit et primae commisit funera pugnae,
deserit Hesperiam et caeli convexa per auras
Iunonem victrix adfatur voce superba:
sentences.l:
And while these things over the plains with even Mars are waged,
of her promise the goddess made mistress, when with blood the war
she had steeped, and had set going the deaths of the first battle,
she leaves Hesperia, and through heaven's vaults, through the airs,
Juno, victorious, she addresses with a voice proud:
sentences.i: And while the fighting goes on over the plains with neither side prevailing, the goddess, her promise made good now that she had steeped the war in blood and brought about the deaths of the first battle, leaves Hesperia, and, passing through the vaults of heaven and the air, speaks to Juno in triumph, in a haughty voice:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Aequo… Marte', 'with even Mars', Mars standing for the fighting (metonymy): the battle hangs even. 'Promissi… facta potens', 'made master of her promise', her task for Juno done; 'potens' takes the genitive, and 'facta' is the perfect participle of 'fio'. 'Ubi… imbuit… commisit', 'when she had steeped… had joined': Latin uses the perfect with 'ubi' where English prefers the pluperfect. 'Sanguine… imbuit', 'wetted with blood'. 'Commisit funera pugnae' turns the phrase 'committere pugnam', 'to join battle', onto the deaths. 'Hesperiam', 'the western land', Italy. 'Caeli convexa per auras': 'per' serves both nouns, 'through the vaults of heaven, through the airs'. The Latin Library prints 'conversa', 'turned about'; Greenough's 'convexa' is translated here. 'Victrix', 'victorious', a feminine agent noun used as an adjective. 'Adfatur', the deponent 'addresses', with Greenough's 'adf-' (familiar 'affatur').

sentences.t: “En, perfecta tibi bello discordia tristi:
sentences.l: “See, made complete for you, by grim war, is discord:
sentences.i: “There: for your sake discord is brought to its fullness, in grim war;
sentences.n: Allecto's speech, proud and mocking. 'En', 'see!', 'look!'. 'Perfecta (est)', 'has been accomplished', with 'est' left out. 'Tibi', dative of advantage, 'for you', at your bidding. 'Bello… tristi', ablative of means, 'by grim war', with 'tristi' agreeing with 'bello', not with 'discordia'. The Fury of discord reports discord done.

sentences.t: dic in amicitiam coeant et foedera iungant.
sentences.l: tell them into friendship to come together and treaties to join.
sentences.i: now tell them to come together in friendship and strike their treaties!
sentences.n: Sarcasm. 'Dic… coeant… iungant', 'tell (them) they should come together… should join', a jussive subjunctive after 'dic' without 'ut', common in speech and poetry; 'coeant' has three syllables, cŏ-ĕ-ant, as at 7.317. 'Foedera iungant', 'join treaties', make alliances: she mocks the league Latinus has offered the Trojans, and the marriage that was to seal it. The subject is Latins and Trojans alike.

sentences.t:
Quando quidem Ausonio respersi sanguine Teucros,
hoc etiam his addam, tua si mihi certa voluntas:
sentences.l:
Since indeed with Ausonian I have spattered blood the Teucrians,
this too to these I will add, if to me sure your will is:
sentences.i: Since I have spattered the Teucrians with Italian blood, I will add this as well, if I can be sure it is your will:
sentences.n: 'Quando quidem', 'since indeed', which Greenough prints as two words (usually 'quandoquidem'). 'Ausonio… sanguine', ablative of means, 'with Italian blood': the Trojans are now stained with the blood of Italians, the guilt that will make peace impossible. 'Respersi', perfect of 'respergo', 'I have spattered'. 'Hoc… his addam', 'I will add this to these (deeds)'. 'Tua si… certa voluntas (est)', 'if your will is certain to me', if I know for sure you want it, with 'si' postponed and 'est' left out; 'mihi' is a dative of reference. The colon announces what she will add.

sentences.i: with rumours I will draw the neighbouring cities into the war and fire their hearts with a passion for the madness of Mars, so that they come from every side to help;
sentences.n: The print has 'veniunt', a misprint for 'veniant', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. 'Ut' here gives the purpose, 'so that they may come', and that needs the subjunctive; the Latin Library prints 'veniant'. 'Finitimas… urbes' framing the line, 'the neighbouring cities'. 'In bella feram', 'I will carry into war', bring them into it. 'Rumoribus', ablative of means, 'with rumours'. 'Insani Martis amore', 'with love of mad Mars', an objective genitive. 'Undique', 'from every side'. 'Auxilio', dative of purpose, 'for help'.

sentences.t: spargam arma per agros.”
sentences.l: I will scatter arms through the fields.”
sentences.i: I will sow weapons all over the countryside.”
sentences.n: 'Spargam', future, 'I will scatter', as a farmer sows seed: a rustic image to end the speech, with no connective (asyndeton). The closing mark ends Allecto's speech.

sentences.t: Tum contra Iuno; “Terrorum et fraudis abunde est;
sentences.l: Then in reply Juno: “Of terrors and of deceit there is plenty;
sentences.i: Then Juno answered: “There has been terror and treachery enough;
sentences.n: Greenough prints a semicolon after 'Iuno', where a colon usually opens a speech (so also 2.733, 'prospiciens; “Nate'); the sense is the same either way, so it is kept as printed, not treated as a misprint. 'Tum contra Iuno', 'then Juno in reply', with the verb of speaking left out, as at 'Aeolus haec contra' (1.76). 'Abunde est', 'there is abundance', 'enough and more': the adverb 'abunde' serves as the predicate, with the partitive genitives 'terrorum et fraudis'. Juno's answer is curt: she wants no more of the Fury.

sentences.t:
stant belli causae, pugnatur comminus armis,
quae fors prima dedit sanguis novus imbuit arma.
sentences.l:
stand fast the causes of war, there is fighting hand to hand with arms,
the arms that chance first gave, fresh blood has stained.
sentences.i: the grounds for war stand firm, they are fighting hand to hand, and the weapons that chance first put into their hands are stained with fresh blood.
sentences.n: 'Stant', 'stand fast', are fixed beyond undoing. 'Pugnatur', impersonal passive, 'there is fighting'. 'Comminus', 'at close quarters'. 'Quae fors prima dedit… arma', 'the arms which chance first gave', the brands and stakes of 505–508: the relative clause comes first, and its antecedent 'arma' waits for the end of the main clause, as the object of 'imbuit'. 'Sanguis novus', 'fresh blood'. 'Imbuit', perfect, 'has stained', picking up 'sanguine bellum imbuit' (541–542). Three clauses with no connectives: asyndeton.

sentences.t:
Talia coniugia et talis celebrent hymenaeos
egregium Veneris genus et rex ipse Latinus.
sentences.l:
Such marriages and such let them celebrate wedding songs,
the illustrious offspring of Venus and the king himself, Latinus.
sentences.i: Let them celebrate marriage and wedding songs of this sort, the illustrious son of Venus and King Latinus himself.
sentences.n: Juno's scorn. 'Celebrent', jussive subjunctive, 'let them celebrate'. 'Talis' = 'tales', accusative plural. 'Hymenaeos', 'wedding songs', named from Hymen, the god of marriage; a Greek word, ending the line in the Greek manner. 'Egregium Veneris genus', 'the illustrious offspring of Venus', Aeneas, 'genus' used of a person, the praise bitter. A wedding paid for in blood: Juno promised Lavinia just that at 7.318, 'sanguine Troiano et Rutulo dotabere, virgo'.

sentences.i: That father, ruler of high Olympus, would not wish you to wander too freely through the upper air: leave this place;
sentences.n: 'Te… errare', accusative and infinitive depending on 'velit'. 'Super aetherias… auras', 'over the upper airs', the bright air of heaven, which is not the Fury's realm. 'Licentius', comparative adverb, 'too freely'. 'Haud… velit', potential subjunctive, 'would not wish'. 'Pater ille', 'that father', Jupiter, kept at a distance by 'ille'. 'Summi regnator Olympi', in apposition. 'Cede locis', 'withdraw from the places', an ablative of separation. Juno sends the Fury home.

sentences.t:
ego, siqua super fortuna laborum est,
ipsa regam. ”Talis dederat Saturnia voces.
sentences.l:
I, if any further fortune of toils there is,
myself will direct it.” Such had given, Saturnia, words.
sentences.i: if there is any further turn in this struggle still to come, I will direct it myself.” Such were the words that Saturnia had spoken.
sentences.n: The print has 'ipsa regam. ”Talis', with a space before the closing mark and none after it, a misprint for 'ipsa regam.” Talis', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. 'Ego… ipsa', 'I… myself', framing the clause with emphasis. 'Siqua', 'if any', Greenough's joined spelling of 'si qua'; after 'si', 'qua' is the indefinite. 'Super… est', 'is left over', 'superest' split in two (tmesis). 'Fortuna laborum', 'fortune of the toils', what the struggle may yet bring. 'Regam', future, 'I will direct'. 'Talis' = 'tales', accusative plural. 'Dederat', pluperfect: the speech is done and the story moves on. 'Voces dare', 'to give words', to speak. 'Saturnia', 'daughter of Saturn', Juno's regular title.

sentences.t:
Illa autem attollit stridentis anguibus alas
Cocytique petit sedem, supera ardua linquens.
sentences.l:
She however raises, hissing with snakes, her wings,
and Cocytus's seeks seat, the upper heights leaving.
sentences.i: She, for her part, lifts her wings, hissing with snakes, and makes for her home by Cocytus, leaving the heights of the world above.
sentences.n: 'Illa', Allecto. 'Stridentis' = 'stridentes', accusative plural agreeing with 'alas', 'whirring', 'hissing'. 'Anguibus', ablative of cause, 'with snakes': her wings, like her hair, writhe with serpents. 'Cocyti… sedem', 'the seat of Cocytus', her dwelling by the river of wailing. 'Supera ardua', 'the high places above', neuter plural adjectives used as nouns. 'Linquens', present participle, 'leaving'.

sentences.t:
Est locus Italiae medio sub montibus altis,
nobilis et fama multis memoratus in oris,
Amsancti valles:
sentences.l:
There is a place in the middle of Italy, under mountains high,
renowned, and by report in many told of regions,
the valley of Amsanctus:
sentences.i: There is a place in the heart of Italy, beneath high mountains, famous and spoken of in many lands, the valley of Amsanctus:
sentences.n: 'Est locus', 'there is a place', the formula that opens the description of a place (an ecphrasis), as at 1.159 'Est in secessu longo locus' and 1.530 'Est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt'. 'Italiae medio', 'in the middle of Italy', 'medio' a neuter noun in the ablative of place. 'Fama… memoratus', 'told of by report' ('fāmā', ablative, long-long). 'Multis… in oris', 'in many regions'. 'Amsancti valles', 'the valley of Amsanctus' ('valles' here is probably the by-form of 'vallis', though it may be plural), a hollow in the Hirpine hills inland from Naples, where a pool gives off deadly sulphurous fumes; it was held to be a mouth of the underworld.

sentences.t:
densis hunc frondibus atrum
urguet utrimque latus nemoris, medioque fragosus
dat sonitum saxis et torto vertice torrens.
sentences.l:
with dense it foliage dark
presses on both sides the flank of a wood, and in its midst a roaring
gives sound on the rocks, with twisting eddy, torrent.
sentences.i: the flank of a forest, dark with thick leaves, hems it in on either side, and through its midst a roaring torrent sounds among the rocks in whirling eddies.
sentences.n: 'Hunc', the place, the object of 'urguet'. 'Densis… frondibus', ablative of cause, 'with dense foliage'. 'Atrum' may go with 'hunc' (the place dark with leaves) or with 'latus' (the wood's dark flank); the sense is the same. 'Urguet', 'presses', 'hems in', Greenough's spelling of 'urget', two syllables, ur-guet. 'Utrimque', 'on both sides'. 'Medio', ablative of place, 'in the middle'. 'Fragosus… torrens' framing the clause, 'the crashing torrent'. 'Saxis', ablative of place, 'on (among) the rocks'. 'Torto vertice', 'with twisted whirl', 'vertex' here an eddy.

sentences.t:
Hic specus horrendum et saevi spiracula Ditis
monstrantur, ruptoque ingens Acheronte vorago
pestiferas aperit fauces, quis condita Erinys,
invisum numen, terras caelumque levabat.
sentences.l:
Here a cave, dreadful, and of savage the breathing-vents, Dis,
are shown, and, Acheron burst through, a vast chasm
its plague-bearing opens jaws, in which hidden the Erinys,
hateful power, earth and heaven relieved.
sentences.i: Here a fearful cave and the breathing vents of cruel Dis are pointed out, and where Acheron has broken through, a vast chasm opens its pestilent jaws; in these the Fury, that hated power, hid herself, and gave earth and heaven relief.
sentences.n: 'Specus horrendum', 'a dreadful cave': 'specus' is usually masculine, but neuter here. 'Spiracula Ditis', 'the breathing-holes of Dis', the vents where the underworld breathes out; Dis is Pluto. 'Monstrantur', 'are shown', pointed out to visitors. 'Rupto… Acheronte', ablative absolute, 'Acheron having burst forth', the river of the underworld breaking through to the surface. 'Ingens… vorago', framing, 'a vast abyss'. 'Pestiferas… fauces', 'plague-bearing jaws'. 'Quis' = 'quibus', an old form of the relative, ablative plural, 'in which'. 'Condita', 'hidden', with middle sense, 'hiding herself'. 'Erinys', the Greek name of a Fury, here Allecto. 'Invisum numen', in apposition, 'a hated power', hated even by her own kin (7.327). 'Levabat', 'was relieving': by sinking out of sight, she freed earth and sky of her presence.

sentences.t:
Nec minus interea extremam Saturnia bello
imponit regina manum.
sentences.l:
No less meanwhile the final, Saturnia, on the war
lays, the queen, hand.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Saturn's daughter, the queen, is no less busy, and puts the finishing hand to the war.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Nec minus', 'no less': there is no slackening once Allecto has gone. 'Extremam… manum', 'the last hand', the finishing touch, as a craftsman sets his last hand to his work; 'imponit… bello', 'puts upon the war', with the dative. 'Saturnia… regina' framing, the queen, daughter of Saturn.

sentences.t:
Ruit omnis in urbem
pastorum ex acie numerus caesosque reportant
Almonem puerum foedatique ora Galaesi
implorantque deos obtestanturque Latinum.
sentences.l:
Rushes the whole into the city,
of herdsmen, from the battle line, number, and the slain they carry back,
Almo the boy and the face of disfigured Galaesus,
and they implore the gods and appeal to Latinus.
sentences.i: The whole company of herdsmen comes rushing from the battle into the city, carrying back their dead, young Almo and Galaesus with his face disfigured, and they call upon the gods and beseech Latinus.
sentences.n: 'Ruit… numerus', 'the number rushes', the whole band: a collective singular, followed by plural verbs ('reportant', 'implorant', 'obtestantur') agreeing with the sense. 'Caesos', 'the slain'. 'Almonem puerum', 'the boy Almo'; 'puer' is used of a young man. 'Foedati… ora Galaesi', 'the face of disfigured Galaesus', the plural 'ora' for one face, as poets use it. 'Obtestantur', deponent, 'call to witness', 'entreat'. The chain of '-que' (polysyndeton) gives the crowd's confusion.

sentences.t:
Turnus adest medioque in crimine caedis et igni
terrorem ingeminat:
sentences.l:
Turnus is there, and in the midst of the outcry of slaughter and the fire
the terror he redoubles:
sentences.i: Turnus is there, and in the thick of the outcry over the killings, in the heat of it all, he redoubles their alarm:
sentences.n: 'Adest', 'is at hand'. 'Medio… in crimine caedis', 'in the middle of the charge of slaughter', while the people cry out against the Trojans for the killings; 'crimen' is 'accusation', 'outcry'. 'Igni', ablative of 'ignis' in '-i', 'fire', the heat of the crowd's passion, and Turnus is burning already with Allecto's torch (7.456–457). 'Ingeminat', 'redoubles'. The colon introduces the gist of his words in indirect speech.

sentences.t:
Teucros in regna vocari,
stirpem admisceri Phrygiam, se limine pelli.
sentences.l:
the Teucrians into the kingdom are being called,
a stock is being mixed in, Phrygian, himself from the threshold driven.
sentences.i: the Teucrians, he says, are being invited to rule, a Phrygian strain is to be mingled with their blood, and he himself is being thrust from the door.
sentences.n: Indirect speech, the verb of saying understood: three accusative-and-infinitive clauses with present passive infinitives, no connectives (asyndeton), each a grievance. 'In regna vocari', 'are being called into the kingdom', invited to royal power. 'Stirpem admisceri Phrygiam', 'a Phrygian stock is being mixed in', through Lavinia's marriage; 'Phrygian' is Trojan, said with contempt. 'Se limine pelli', 'that he is being driven from the threshold', shut out of the house where he was the promised son-in-law; 'se' refers to Turnus, the speaker.

sentences.t:
Tum quorum attonitae Baccho nemora avia matres
insultant thiasis (neque enim leve nomen Amatae),
undique collecti coeunt Martemque fatigant.
sentences.l:
Then they whose, struck by Bacchus, through pathless groves mothers
leap in revel bands (for not light is the name of Amata),
from all sides gathered come together and weary Mars.
sentences.i: Then those whose mothers, struck mad by Bacchus, go leaping through the trackless woods in their revel bands (for the name of Amata carries weight) gather from every side and come together, and weary Mars with their demands.
sentences.n: 'Quorum… matres', 'whose mothers', the women Amata led into the woods (385–405); the antecedent, 'they', is left out and is the subject of 'coeunt'. 'Attonitae Baccho', 'thunderstruck by Bacchus', possessed; ablative of cause. 'Nemora avia', 'the pathless groves', accusative with 'insultant', 'leap upon', 'dance over'. 'Thiasis', ablative, 'in their thiasi', the Greek word for Bacchic revel bands. 'Neque enim leve nomen Amatae (est)', 'for the name of Amata is not light', a parenthesis: the queen's name carries weight. 'Coeunt' has three syllables, cŏ-ĕ-unt. 'Collecti', masculine: the men, sons and husbands of those women. 'Martem fatigant', 'they weary Mars', they call on him and clamour for war without rest.

sentences.t:
Ilicet infandum cuncti contra omina bellum,
contra fata deum perverso numine poscunt,
certatim regis circumstant tecta Latini.
sentences.i: At once, all of them, against the omens and against the fates of the gods, under a power that turns all awry, demand an accursed war, and crowd eagerly round the palace of King Latinus.
sentences.n: 'Ilicet', 'forthwith', 'at once', literally 'ire licet', 'you may go', the formula that dismissed an assembly. 'Infandum… bellum' framing the line, 'an unspeakable war'. 'Contra… contra', anaphora: the omens (the bees and the fire in Lavinia's hair, 7.59–80) and the oracle of Faunus (7.96–101) forbid it. 'Deum' = 'deorum', the old genitive plural. 'Perverso numine', 'with perverse divinity', under a power that wrenches things from their course, Juno's working against the fates. 'Certatim', 'in rivalry', 'eagerly'. 'Regis… tecta Latini', framing, 'the house of King Latinus'. No connective before 'certatim': asyndeton.

sentences.t:
Ille velut pelagi rupes immota resistit,
ut pelagi rupes magno veniente fragore,
quae sese multis circum latrantibus undis
mole tenet; scopuli nequiquam et spumea circum
saxa fremunt laterique inlisa refunditur alga.
sentences.l:
He, like a sea's rock unmoved, resists,
like a sea's rock, when a great crash comes on,
which itself, with many waves barking round,
by its mass holds; the crags in vain and the foaming around
rocks roar, and, dashed against its side, the seaweed is washed back.
sentences.i: He stands firm like a rock in the sea that will not move, like a rock in the sea when a great crash of waves comes on, which holds itself fast by its own mass while wave upon wave barks round it; the crags and the foaming reefs roar about it in vain, and the weed flung against its side is washed back again.
sentences.n: The simile of the rock. 'Velut… ut', 'like… like', the opening of the line taken up again with a slight change (epanalepsis) to dwell on the image. Some take the two lines for alternative drafts left in the unrevised poem; Greenough prints both. 'Immota', 'unmoved'. 'Magno veniente fragore', ablative absolute, 'a great crash coming'. 'Sese… mole tenet', 'holds itself by its mass'. 'Multis… latrantibus undis', ablative absolute, 'many waves barking round', the sea as a pack of dogs. 'Circum', adverb, twice. 'Nequiquam', 'in vain'. 'Lateri inlisa', 'dashed against its side', dative with a compound; 'inlisa' keeps 'in-' unassimilated (familiar 'illisa'). 'Refunditur', 'is poured back'. The model is Iliad 15.618–621, where the Greeks hold like a great sheer rock by the grey sea, enduring winds and swollen waves. Latinus's rock, though, will hold only for himself.

sentences.t:
Verum ubi nulla datur caecum exsuperare potestas
consilium et saevae nutu Iunonis eunt res,
multa deos aurasque pater testatus inanis:
sentences.l:
But when no is given the blind to overcome power
purpose, and by the nod of savage Juno things go,
many times the gods and the airs, the father, having called to witness, empty:
sentences.i: But when no power is given him to overcome their blind purpose, and things go as cruel Juno wills, the old father, calling the gods and the empty air again and again to witness, cries:
sentences.n: 'Verum', 'but'. 'Nulla… potestas', 'no power', with the infinitive 'exsuperare', 'to overcome', depending on it. 'Caecum… consilium', 'the blind counsel', their reckless purpose. 'Nutu', 'by the nod': a god's nod is his will. 'Eunt res', 'things go'. 'Multa', neuter plural as an adverb, 'much', 'often' (an internal accusative). 'Testatus', perfect participle of the deponent 'testor', active in sense, 'calling to witness'. 'Auras… inanis', 'the empty airs', with 'inanis' = 'inanes', accusative plural: the air that cannot help. 'Pater', 'the father', Latinus, father of his people and of Lavinia.

sentences.t: “Frangimur heu fatis, inquit, ferimurque procella!
sentences.l: “We are broken, alas, by the fates,” he says, “and swept along by the storm!
sentences.i: “We are shattered, alas, by fate,” he says, “and carried off by the storm!
sentences.n: Greenough, as usual, prints no marks round an 'inquit' that falls inside a speech (so 1.754, 8.351); l and i add them. 'Fātis' is long-long, 'fĕrĭmur' short-short. 'Frangimur… ferimurque', present passives, 'we are broken… and borne along': the image turns from the rock to a ship wrecked in a gale. 'Fatis', ablative of means. 'Procella', 'the storm', of the war. 'Heu', 'alas'.

sentences.t:
Ipsi has sacrilego pendetis sanguine poenas,
O miseri.
sentences.l:
You yourselves these with sacrilegious will pay blood penalties,
O wretched ones.
sentences.i: You yourselves will pay the penalty for this with your sacrilegious blood, you poor wretches.
sentences.n: 'Ipsi', 'you yourselves', set first for emphasis. 'Poenas pendere', 'to pay penalties', literally 'to weigh them out', from payment in weighed metal. 'Sacrilego… sanguine', ablative of price, 'with sacrilegious blood', the blood of men who defy the gods. 'O miseri', vocative, 'O wretched men'; Greenough prints the capital O even inside a sentence.

sentences.t:
Te, Turne, nefas, te triste manebit
supplicium, votisque deos venerabere seris.
sentences.l:
You, Turnus, the guilt, you a grim will await
punishment, and with vows the gods you will worship, late.
sentences.i: You, Turnus, your crime will wait for, you a bitter punishment, and you will pray to the gods with vows that come too late.
sentences.n: 'Te… te', anaphora, the repeated pronoun pointing at Turnus. 'Nefas', 'the impious thing', the guilt of this war, which will 'wait for' him; 'manebit' takes 'te' as a direct object. 'Triste… supplicium', 'grim punishment', framing the line-end. 'Venerabere' = 'veneraberis', future of the deponent 'veneror', with '-re' for '-ris' in the second person, a common form. 'Votis… seris', 'with late vows', ablative of means: prayers made too late. The words look ahead to Turnus's end in Book XII.

sentences.t: Nam mihi parta quies, omnisque in limine portus;
sentences.l: For to me won is rest, and all at the entrance is the harbour;
sentences.i: For my rest is won; I stand at the very mouth of the harbour;
sentences.n: 'Mihi parta (est) quies', 'rest has been won for me', a dative of advantage: he is old and near his end. 'Quies' has two syllables, quĭ-ēs; 'parta' has a short final a. 'Omnisque in limine portus (est)', 'and all the harbour is at the entrance': the whole of his haven lies just ahead, death being the harbour, the ship-image again. 'Omnis' is nominative singular, agreeing with 'portus'.

sentences.t:
funere felici spolior. ”Nec plura locutus
saepsit se tectis rerumque reliquit habenas.
sentences.l:
of a happy funeral I am robbed.” Nor more having spoken,
he walled himself in his house and let go of affairs the reins.
sentences.i: all I am robbed of is a happy funeral.” He said no more, but shut himself up in his palace and let fall the reins of state.
sentences.n: The print has 'spolior. ”Nec', with a space before the closing mark and none after it, a misprint for 'spolior.” Nec', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. 'Spolior', present passive, 'I am robbed', with the ablative of separation 'funere felici': a happy funeral, a death in peace, with his kingdom whole and honours paid. The closing mark ends Latinus's speech. 'Nec plura locutus', 'not having said more', the perfect participle of the deponent 'loquor', active in sense. 'Saepsit se tectis', 'fenced himself in his house', from 'saepio', 'to hedge in'; 'tectis' is ablative of place. 'Rerum… habenas', 'the reins of affairs', the government: the charioteer lets the reins drop. 'Reliquit', 'let go', 'abandoned'. Latinus will not declare the war; in the next part Juno opens its gates herself.
